title: Slide 1 · Deep Learning and Representation Learning
question: The four readings are [1, 1, 3, 3]. What does a unit with weights [−1, +1] and zero bias output on the middle pair, before and after ReLU?
answer: On [1, 3] the weighted sum is −1 × 1 + 1 × 3 = 2. ReLU keeps positive values, so the output is 2. The unit measures an increase in brightness.

title: Slide 2 · What information survives an average?
question: Could a complicated classifier recover the changes from just these two means?
answer: No. It receives the same input value 2 in both cases. It would need another measurement or a more informative representation.

title: Slide 3 · Slide one detector along the record
question: Why does the shape have two channels but only three time positions?
answer: We used two filters. Each filter has three places where its entire two-reading window fits. The batch still contains one record.

title: Slide 4 · Combine the strongest rise and fall
question: What ambiguity remains if the final unit sees only [strongest rise, strongest fall]?
answer: It cannot tell when either occurred. A rise followed by a fall and a fall followed by a rise can give the same two magnitudes. A task that depends on order needs a representation that retains position.

title: Slide 5 · What does depth buy?
question: Why would two affine layers lack this behavior?
answer: Substituting a₁t + b₁ into a₂u + b₂ gives (a₂a₁)t + (a₂b₁ + b₂), still a straight line. ReLU introduces the bend that lets another stage split the response again.

title: Slide 6 · Learn a detector from examples
question: Why could these three training cases teach the gain but tell us little about falling light?
answer: All three changes are positive. They constrain the response to increases. Evaluating falls would require falling examples and a representation that can express the desired falling response.

title: Slide 7 · Compare readings on a common scale
question: Why keep the original training mean when a new bright lamp is measured?
answer: The model learned in the original coordinate system. Recomputing the scale from the evaluation records would change that system and use information from the evaluation set.

title: Slide 8 · Trace a fading gradient
question: What would repeated local slopes of 2 do at depth six?
answer: They multiply to 2⁶ = 64. The sensitivity grows. Both very small and very large gradients can make training difficult.

title: Slide 9 · Add a route for the input
question: If F(x) = −x, does the direct route guarantee a nonzero gradient?
answer: No. The two slopes add to 1 − 1 = 0. A direct route can help gradients travel but the learned correction still matters.

title: Slide 10 · Choose an update you can check
question: Why is one training-loss reduction insufficient evidence for choosing a model?
answer: It measures the fit on the same observation used for the update. Compare learning behavior over multiple steps and evaluate candidate models on separate validation records.

title: Slide 11 · Train two convolutional layers and inspect their features
question: The model gets six of six right and the rule “always changing” gets four of six. Which part of the result suggests that training changed the representation? What remains untested?
answer: For the rising example, the second pooled feature changes from about 0.25 to 8.69, while the same feature stays at zero for the steady example. This particular distinction becomes stronger during training. The six predictions test new levels and jump sizes at a fixed jump position. They give no measured result for gradual changes, sensor noise or a jump at another position.

title: Slide 13 · From this module to the next
question: Which part of [2, 4, 6] could supply a target if we show the model only the first two readings?
answer: The original last reading, 6, is already recorded. We can hide it from the input and use it to score a prediction. How well that task teaches useful features will depend on the patterns in the records.

title: Office hours · What makes an intermediate number a feature?
question: What makes an intermediate number a feature?
answer: Its role in the next computation. The filter output 2 describes a local rise and becomes input to a later unit. The same number could be a final answer in a task that asks only for the size of that rise.

title: Office hours · Does every hidden neuron have a name people can recognize?
question: Does every hidden neuron have a name people can recognize?
answer: We chose filter weights that expose a simple pattern. Learned features can mix several patterns, and changing units together can preserve a network’s predictions. Inspect responses to controlled input changes before assigning an interpretation.

title: Office hours · Will adding more layers always improve my results?
question: Will adding more layers always improve my results?
answer: Depth can reuse and compose features. Useful performance also depends on data, optimization and evaluation. Compare depths with the same train/validation split, inspect losses and record whether performance on new records improves.

title: Office hours · How is input scaling related to normalization inside a network?
question: How is input scaling related to normalization inside a network?
answer: Both put numbers on a useful scale. Here we fixed training-set statistics for an input feature. A layer such as LayerNorm instead computes statistics across specified features of each input example. The axes and the moment when statistics are computed matter.

title: Exercise 1
question: Two four-reading records have strongest rise 3 and strongest fall 2, but reach their peaks at different times. Can a classifier using only those two features tell which peaked first?
answer: Both inputs are [3, 2], so any fixed classifier receives identical evidence. Retain a time coordinate or ordered sequence of features to answer the question.

title: Exercise 2
question: Apply the two filters to [3, 1, 2, 2]. Give the hidden channel values and the score for the readout r + f − 2.5.
answer: Differences are [−2, 1, 0]. Rise channel [0, 1, 0], fall channel [2, 0, 0]. Maxima are 1 and 2. The score is 0.5.

title: Exercise 3
question: Five filters scan a batch of three length-8 signals with one input channel. Each filter spans three readings. With unit step and no padding, what shape reaches the next layer?
answer: A window can start at positions 1 through 6. There are three records and five filters, so the output shape is [3, 5, 6].

title: Exercise 4
question: In the triangular network, evaluate g(0.375) and then g(g(0.375)).
answer: g(0.375) = 0.75. Then g(0.75) = 2 × 0.75 − 4 × 0.25 = 0.5. The second layer transforms a response from the first layer.

title: Exercise 5
question: Each of three correction branches has local slope −0.2. Compare the gradient multiplier with and without an identity route around each branch.
answer: Plain multiplier (−0.2)³ = −0.008. Residual multiplier (1 − 0.2)³ = 0.512. The sign and magnitude both change.

title: Exercise 6
question: Train on readings 2 and 6, which have population standard deviation 2. Standardize a held-out reading of 8. Why avoid fitting a new scale to this single reading?
answer: The training mean is 4, so z = (8 − 4)/2 = 2. A scale fitted on a single value has zero spread and incorporates the very observation intended for evaluation.

title: Exercise 7
question: Trace the two-convolution classifier on six test records. What is the tensor shape after the second ReLU? Propose a test of whether the detector recognizes a jump that occurs one reading earlier.
answer: The shape is [6, 3, 2]. Keep the fitted model frozen, and move the jump from between readings 2 and 3 to between readings 1 and 2. For instance, replace a rising [2.5, 2.5, 5.5, 5.5] with [2.5, 5.5, 5.5, 5.5]. Evaluate both rising and falling shifts and steady controls. Report the changed-position results separately.

title: Module overview · Deep Learning and Representation Learning
question: What is this module about?
answer:
Deep Learning and Representation Learning. By the end of this module, you should be able to:
• Explain how depth changes the functions a model can express.
• Implement a small deep network and inspect intermediate features.
• Recognize vanishing gradients and the purpose of residual connections.
quote:
